Unfortunately this introduces the exact issue that the timeout was added to solve. MessageContactsRaw is used indirectly to populate the LHS and RHS of the messages tab. This request must not be allowed to complete after a navigation change.

Because the Changes listener in MessagesCtrl passes in the `changes` option we can tell in updateContacts that we could pass in { timeout: false } to MessageContact. Then we'd have to check in the callback that no navigation had occurred.

Another possible solution - the `{ timeout: false }` option is used mainly in the root scope because you can't navigate away from the root scope and still be in the app. I think #925 occurs when the user changes from route `messages.a` to `messages.b`. In this case you haven't navigated away from the parent `messages` route, but you would want to cancel all requests that would affect the view of the child `messages.a` route.

In essence you only want to cancel requests made by a route you're navigating away from - if you still within Messages but have changed the selected Message then anything that would update the LHS should be allowed to continue, but anything that would update the RHS should be cancelled. Likewise if you're navigating to Reports anything that updates the overall Inbox should be allowed to continue but anything that updates the Messages LHS or RHS should be cancelled.

So the more correct solution would be for every call to the HttpWrapper to provide the route which will be updated. Then when a route change event occurs pass in the new route ( https://github.com/angular-ui/ui-router/wiki#state-change-events ), and only cancel requests that aren't part of the new route.

For bonus points instead of passing in the route, HttpWrapper can query $state.$current to automatically determine the correct state.

This is quite complex but will probably solve this issue and a bunch of other ones we haven't found yet. It also removes the hacky `timeout: false` option.

Note that `if` statements have a very small subset of functions that are allowed to be part of the guard expression, and `proplists:get_value` is not one of them. Happy to change it if you think the following code is more readable:

``` erlang
<<"data_record">> ->
  KujuaMessage = proplists:get_value(<<"kujua_message">>, Doc),
  if
    KujuaMessage ->
      Tasks = proplists:get_value(<<"tasks">>, Doc, []),
      if
        length(Tasks) > 0 ->
          % Outgoing message
          Ok(
            proplists:get_value(<<"contact">>,
              element(1, hd(proplists:get_value(<<"messages">>,
                element(1, hd(Tasks)))))));
        true ->
          false
      end;
    true ->
      % Incoming message
      Ok(proplists:get_value(<<"contact">>, Doc))
  end;
```

Note that while in theory we could pull the Tasks var up by one and then go `if KujuaMessage andAlso length(Tasks) > 0` I'd be worried about perf in pulling out tasks when it's not necessary. Note that I have no idea if doing that function call is actually slow, it's probably not. Would need to be tested.

I was all set to say "I understand the theory as to why this would be slow for a contiguously-allocated region of memory, but surely that's not the case for a modern Javascript engine"... then I benchmarked it: http://jsperf.com/splice-dir. Unless I messed something up, there's a massive performance difference for large lists.

When adding or removing elements from an array you have to do it in reverse, because otherwise when you remove an element the next `i` is wrong. You either have to update `i` inside the loop which is confusing and buggy or work in reverse so you only modify indexes of elements you've already checked. Using Dave's performance example, the two cases will produce different arrays (which is probably why the performance is so different) - the forward case will remove every second element, and the reverse case will remove every element.

I understand the concept of code reuse, but reusing code for things that are actually not using it is just adding obscurity to me. It increases the number of functions applied to all cases (since all actions have to be applied to all cases), and makes it harder to understand what the action does (because they're used outside of the necessary case : it's harder to understand e.g. why you're fetching children for a type person that you know has no children)
It also makes it harder to make changes later, because now all cases will use this function, and so if I want to make a change for, say, the `person` case, I risk changing the case for, say, `clinic`.

My understandings:

 - `.getTime()` returns the number of millis since 1970 UTC. So it doesn't care about timezones.

 - `new Date()` creates a date by storing the number of millis since 1970 UTC, but formats and is interacted with based on the system timezone.

So `result` ends up being the local representation of whatever date was passed (which will *also* probably be the local representation depending on how it was created from the database, but this code being defensive and re-creating it with the # millis since 1970 UTC is not bad).

It's a way of grouping stuff together. Say if we're showing a list of reports and some are expanded and some are not we can either store `expanded: true` on the db doc itself or create a new wrapper object (which I'm calling a model) and store `{ doc: doc, expanded: true }`. This has a couple of advantages - it keeps the db doc the same as what you see in the db, and it means we can use optimistic locking properly and not worry about accidentally persisting the `expanded: true` property. It also means we can have a model generator that produces an object which can be consumed by a generic template for use on multiple pages, so we don't have each controller doing its own thing.

Any user utilising this feature will have a hardware fingerprint reader with _Simprints_ written on it, so I'd hazard that using the brand name is appropriate.

There are quite a few bugs with the async code flow here...

1. This callback is executed _before_ the migration is complete because it's not waiting for the async code to complete. This will cause a race condition in the app, but will also mean API starts up even if this migration fails (it should not).
2. The `return callback` statements in the `forEach` loops don't return from the migration function - they return from the function given to the `forEach` call. This means the callback may be invoked multiple times which isn't expected by the API startup code.

I recommend when you change this code to use PouchDB you use promises instead of callbacks. One of the reasons I really dislike callbacks is it's really easy to make these sorts of errors (I do it all the time). Once you're using Promises you can do things like `return Promise.all(myAsyncFunctions);` to make sure the Promise doesn't resolve until all the requests have completed.

It's not ideal to get the doc before updating it. CouchDB uses optimistic locking to ensure that two users don't update the same doc at the same time. It does this by having the `_rev` field which changes every time you edit the doc and if the given `_rev` doesn't match then it fails your request with a `409` (conflict). This is a good thing because it means if someone else has updated the doc you don't overwrite their changes.

So, you should be able to just call `DB().put($scope.doc)` and it'll work if you're editing an up to date document, and it'll fail if you're editing an old version.

So this was intentional on my part, but I have been wrong before! We should have philosophical conversations once we're back from the holidays.

I just added a piece of code I planned to do next year around code execution, as it makes my intentions clearer. The situation is now:
 - If there is a parsing error the app doesn't start
 - If there is a execution error the app logs and error[1] and moves on to the next set

The reasoning behind this is:
 - We want to reduce the amount of incorrect / broken configuration in production in general
 - And here especially, as in this instance it would mean people think they are purging when they are not
 - On the one hand we shouldn't stop people from using the app
 - And on the other hand errors just logged to the console are highly likely to be ignored

So:
 - If there is a bad config we can **always** detect we should hard error so it will definitely be caught in testing. We have this philosophy in other places, such as api startup forcing you to have CouchDB configured correctly before it starts.
 - If there is bad config we can only sometimes detect (eg function execution based on parameters etc) we shouldn't hard error, because we aren't confident it will always happen, and so there is a much greater chance it will exist in production.

One addendum here that goes against my reasoning a little is that a hard error could occur because of JS feature support, which may pass if they use their local Chrome and do not also test against the phone app (which is locked to the right version). It is probably conceivable (unfortunately) that people would think to test locally, but not on the device.

[1] I am considering taking the execution errors and putting them somewhere feedback can find them on startup and send out. Maybe that's too extra though?

Hard failures are good but only if the phone can recover when the error is fixed on the server. Unless I've missed something if the function fails to compile then potentially every phone will have to be brought back to base and wiped and everything downloaded again. This failure is _too_ hard.

I'm happy with the app not starting up, but only if it can be fixed remotely without IT support. I can't think of any easy way to do that. Maybe starting the app with a parameter which runs replication but obscures the UI. Then when the settings are changed the dialog will show, the user can refresh, and be up and running again.

Imagine this:
You have a `pregnancy` form which adds a `Pregnancy Visit Schedule`.

There is a potential bug here. Firstly `JSON.stringify` is not deterministic so you may get properties in a different order (if you upgrade Node for example). Secondly I'm not sure our payload generation will be deterministic either. 

I'm not sure how to solve this without deep sorting the object properties. Consider using this library: https://www.npmjs.com/package/object-hash

Awesome catch. I wasn't aware that stringify wasn't deterministic, but you're right it definitely is at least based on how the object gets constructed, which if anything we could accidentally change pretty easily.

So what are your thoughts on:
```js
const hash = payload => require('object-hash')(JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(payload)));
```

Notes:
 - `stringify` then `parse` to make sure it's the contents that would be sent over the wire that we're hashing, not stuff that wouldn't make it.
 - all the default options seem good to me, and I presume they wouldn't be so bold as to change defaults without also bumping a major

The other option is that we just store the entire JSON object with no hashing at all, and use a deep equality check instead of checking the hash. The upside is that this is *also* nice from a logging / debugging / analysis perspective, as you can see and debug what was sent. The downsides are the obvious ones around doc size, esp in situations where we are keeping docs maybe aggressively in sync. We could purge them after they are needed (ie if you sent A,B,A you don't need to keep the first A) but then you arguably lose some of the pros because you can't see the whole history. The title **shouldn't be set in effect & store,** it's something that every page should be able to define freely. 
If in the future we add a new content component (page), 'contact new borns', then we need to add another condition here for the title to work properly, similar to what happened with 'contact decease', because effects aren't necessarily specific of a page. With the change to line 174 this function is async and a caller is expecting to await a call to saveFormToDb (this function) and having this return statement return a promise is desirable, rather than this doing the await. As coded here the call to `db.putAttachment` will [return a promise](https://pouchdb.com/api.html#save_attachment) and the `await` will wait for that promise to be resolved to yield a "real value". Since this function is an `await` function though, it will be wrapped in a new already-resolved promise and that is what will be returned. The difference is small, but the preferred approach is only to `await` a call if you need to use the result of it. If not, return that promise and let other code `await` it, which that other code would already be required to do given this is an `async` function.
